messages.changelog.v2.1: A new dashboard with live status, a plain-language diagnosis, a latency chart, jitter, packet loss, and availability for today, 7 days and 30 days.
messages.changelog.v2.2: A History screen with a log for each day, filters, and CSV export for one day, 7 days or 30 days.
messages.changelog.v2.3: A monthly report page with “Print or save as PDF”, ready to send to your internet provider.
messages.changelog.v2.4: A Speed test screen with a live gauge, today's runs, scheduled tests and an alert threshold.
messages.changelog.v2.5: Dark and light themes with a circular reveal when you switch, plus full Arabic and English with a right-to-left layout.
messages.changelog.v2.6: In-app pages: What's new, FAQ, Privacy and Terms of use.
messages.changelog.v2.7: A new, gentler default alert sound.
messages.changelog.v2.8: Settings shows whether your custom sound is active and how long it is, with “Try the sound” and “Play like a real alert”.

messages.changelog.v2.10: The layout works in phone-size windows.
messages.changelog.v2.11: Uploaded custom alert sounds silently fell back to the default. Uploads are now checked and converted, and the sound you upload is the one that plays.
messages.changelog.v2.12: The auto-updater no longer picks the window (GUI) build for a tray install.
messages.changelog.v2.13: The dashboard is reachable only from this computer and needs a private key that changes daily, so an open dashboard reconnects on its own after the app restarts. Open it from the tray menu or the app window.
messages.changelog.v2.14: Your webhook URL and Telegram token are never sent back to the browser. Settings shows them as “Saved — hidden”.

messages.changelog.v2.16: Updates download only from GitHub, and the Go networking and crypto libraries were updated.
messages.changelog.v2.17: Notification controls: turn the sound on or off and set its volume, set quiet hours, pick which events go to desktop, webhook or Telegram, skip short outages, and get reminders while the connection stays down.
messages.changelog.v2.18: A notification bell and a Notifications page that list every alert, where it was sent, and what was held back and why.
messages.changelog.v2.19: Windows alerts show the connection status icon and an Open button, and a new connection alert replaces the previous one instead of piling up.
messages.changelog.v2.20: Webhook and Telegram messages are written in the app's language.

messages.faq.what.a: It checks your connection every few seconds in three ways: it connects to DNS servers, loads a small web page, and looks up website names. Every outage is saved with its exact start time, how long it lasted, and which part failed. You can then turn that into a report for your internet provider.
messages.faq.open.q: How do I open the dashboard?
messages.faq.open.a: Click the tray icon and choose “Open dashboard”, or use the app window if you installed the window version. Typing the address into the browser yourself shows a locked page, because the dashboard needs a key that changes every time the app starts.
messages.faq.platforms.q: Does it work on macOS and Linux?
messages.faq.platforms.a: Yes. There are builds for Windows, macOS and Linux. The “Start with Windows” option only exists on Windows.
messages.faq.free.a: Yes. It's open source under the MIT license, free for personal and commercial use. There's no account and nothing to sign up for.
messages.faq.disconnected.q: When does it say I'm disconnected?
messages.faq.disconnected.a: When checks fail 3 times in a row. With the default 5-second interval, that's about 15 seconds. This keeps a single lost check from counting as an outage. You can change both numbers in Settings → Monitoring.
messages.faq.unstable.a: You're online, but the connection is poor: more than 20% of packets are lost, or responses take longer than 500 ms. Both limits can be changed in Settings → Monitoring.
messages.faq.layers.q: What's the difference between a DNS problem and a full outage?
messages.faq.layers.a: A full outage means nothing gets through. A DNS problem means the line works but website names can't be looked up, so pages don't open. A website problem means names resolve but pages don't load. The History screen and the report show which one happened, which is useful when your provider says “the line was fine”.
messages.faq.router.q: Is the problem my router or my provider?
messages.faq.router.a: The app also checks your router (the local gateway). If the router answers but the internet doesn't, the diagnosis points to your provider. If the router doesn't answer either, the problem is in your home network: Wi-Fi, cables, or the router itself.
messages.faq.targets.q: Can I change what it checks?
messages.faq.targets.a: Yes. Settings → Check targets has three lists: DNS servers (8.8.8.8 and 1.1.1.1 by default), web pages, and names to look up. Each list holds up to 10 entries, and you can test them before saving.
messages.faq.data.q: How much internet data does it use?
messages.faq.data.a: Regular checks are tiny: a connection, an empty web page and a name lookup. Speed tests are different. A test moves as much data as your line can in its time limit, so on a fast connection one test can use hundreds of megabytes. If your data is limited, don't schedule automatic speed tests.
messages.faq.where.a: As a system notification with a sound on this computer. You can also send them to a Discord or Slack channel with a webhook, or to Telegram. Set these up in Settings → Alerts and use the test button to make sure they arrive.
messages.faq.telegram.q: How do I set up Telegram alerts?
messages.faq.telegram.a: Create a bot with @BotFather in Telegram and copy its token. Send your bot any message, then find your chat ID. Paste both into Settings → Alerts and press the test button.
messages.faq.sound.q: Why isn't my custom sound playing?
messages.faq.sound.a: Open Settings → Sound. It shows whether your own sound is in use and how long it is. Files must be MP3 or WAV, up to 30 seconds and 10 MB. “Play like a real alert” plays it exactly as an alert would. If you hear nothing, check that the computer isn't muted.
messages.faq.silent.q: I didn't get a notification on Windows. Why?
messages.faq.silent.a: Windows hides notifications while Do not disturb or Focus is on, and it lets you turn them off per app. Check Settings → System → Notifications in Windows. The outage is still saved in History either way.
messages.faq.quiet.a: In Settings → Notifications, turn on Quiet hours and choose the times and days. You can mute only the sound or hold desktop alerts completely. A window that crosses midnight, like 22:00 to 07:00, counts for the day it starts. Webhook and Telegram messages are still sent, and every alert is still saved.
messages.faq.noise.q: Can I stop alerts for very short drops?
messages.faq.noise.a: Yes. Set “Wait before alerting” in Settings → Notifications. Outages shorter than that are saved in History but don't alert you. “Remind while down” repeats the alert every few minutes until the connection comes back.
messages.faq.history.q: Where can I see past notifications?
messages.faq.history.a: Click the bell at the top, or open Notifications in the menu. Each alert shows where it was sent and, if something was held back, the reason, such as quiet hours or a channel you turned off. The app keeps the latest 500.
messages.faq.proof.q: How do I send proof to my internet provider?
messages.faq.proof.a: In History, press “Monthly report” and choose “Print or save as PDF”. It lists every outage with its time, duration and cause. For raw data, export CSV from History for one day, 7 days or 30 days.
messages.faq.retention.q: How long is my history kept?
messages.faq.retention.a: 90 days. Older log files are deleted automatically. The logs live in the “logs” folder next to the app. Choose “Open logs folder” from the tray menu to find them.
messages.faq.speedserver.q: Which server does the speed test use?
messages.faq.speedserver.a: Cloudflare's speed test servers by default. You can point it at other servers in Settings → Speed test.
messages.faq.schedule.q: Can speed tests run on their own?
messages.faq.schedule.a: Yes. Set an interval in Settings → Speed test. You can also set a minimum speed. Results are sent to your Discord, Slack or Telegram alerts, and a result below that speed is marked as too slow.
messages.faq.send.q: Does it send my data anywhere?
messages.faq.send.a: No. There's no account, no tracking and no analytics. The only connections it makes are the checks themselves, speed tests, update checks on GitHub, and the Discord, Slack or Telegram alerts you set up. The Privacy page lists each one.
messages.faq.lan.q: Can someone else on my network open the dashboard?
messages.faq.lan.a: No. The dashboard only accepts connections from this computer, and even then it needs the key the app creates each time it starts.
messages.faq.secrets.a: In config.json next to the app. Your webhook URL and Telegram token are saved there as plain text, so don't share that file or that folder. The dashboard never sends them back to the browser.
messages.faq.updates.a: The app checks GitHub for a new version every 6 hours, or right away when you press “Check for updates”. Before installing, it checks the download against the release's checksums. Test (pre-release) versions are never offered automatically.
messages.faq.bug.q: I found a bug. Where do I report it?
messages.faq.bug.a: Open an issue on the project's GitHub page. Say what you expected, what happened, and your app version (shown at the bottom of the sidebar). Don't paste your config.json, since it may contain your webhook or token. You can also reach us on WhatsApp, Discord or email from the Contact page.
messages.privacy.intro: Internet Monitor runs on your computer and keeps your data there. This page lists everything it stores and every place it connects to.
messages.privacy.short.title: The short version
messages.privacy.short.p1: There's no account, no analytics, no ads and no tracking. The people who make Internet Monitor can't see your history, your settings or your alerts.
messages.privacy.stored.title: What's stored on your computer
messages.privacy.stored.p1: Everything is kept in the app's folder, except two small preferences kept by your browser.
messages.privacy.stored.li1: config.json: your settings. This includes your webhook URL, Telegram token and chat ID, saved as plain text. Don't share this file.
messages.privacy.stored.li2: The logs folder: every check, outage and speed test result, plus app.log, a diagnostic log of what the app did. Files older than 90 days are deleted automatically.
messages.privacy.stored.li3: notification.wav: your custom alert sound, if you uploaded one.
messages.privacy.stored.li4: .session: the dashboard key for the current launch. It's replaced every time the app starts.
messages.privacy.stored.li5: Your browser remembers your theme and language, so the dashboard opens the way you left it.
messages.privacy.network.title: What leaves your computer
messages.privacy.network.p1: The app only connects to the places below. Each of them sees your IP address, as with any internet connection, and its own privacy policy applies.
messages.privacy.network.li1: Connection checks go to the targets in Settings → Check targets. By default: Google and Cloudflare DNS servers (8.8.8.8 and 1.1.1.1), connectivitycheck.gstatic.com, and name lookups for www.google.com and www.cloudflare.com. It also checks your own router.
messages.privacy.network.li2: Speed tests go to speed.cloudflare.com by default, and only when you start one or schedule them. The test data contains nothing that identifies your device.
messages.privacy.network.li3: Update checks go to GitHub (api.github.com) every 6 hours, or when you press “Check for updates”. Installing an update downloads it from GitHub.
messages.privacy.network.li4: Alerts go to Discord, Slack or Telegram only if you set them up. They contain the status, times, durations and causes of outages, or a speed test result. The app doesn't add your computer's name or IP address.
messages.privacy.dashboard.title: The dashboard
messages.privacy.dashboard.p1: The dashboard is served by the app on this computer (127.0.0.1). Other devices on your network can't open it. It uses one cookie, which holds the key for the current launch. It loads no outside scripts, fonts or images.
messages.privacy.control.title: You're in control
messages.privacy.control.p1: You can delete the logs folder at any time to erase your history. Deleting config.json resets your settings. To remove the app completely, turn off “Start with Windows” in Settings → App, quit the app, and delete its folder.
messages.privacy.changes.title: Changes to this page
messages.privacy.changes.p1: If a new version changes what the app stores or where it connects, this page is updated and the change is listed in What's new. The date at the top shows the last update.
messages.privacy.contact.title: Questions
messages.privacy.contact.p1: Reach us through any channel on the Contact page. Don't send your config.json or logs unless we ask, since they may contain your webhook, token or history.
messages.terms.intro: Internet Monitor is free, open-source software under the MIT license. This page explains what that means in plain language. If anything here differs from the license, the license applies.
messages.terms.use.title: What you may do
messages.terms.use.p1: You may use Internet Monitor for free, at home or at work. You may also copy, change, share, or sell copies of it. When you share it or a changed version, keep the copyright and license notice with it.
messages.terms.warranty.title: No warranty

IN NO EVENT SHALL THE AUTHORS OR COPYRIGHT HOLDERS BE LIABLE FOR ANY CLAIM, DAMAGES OR OTHER LIABILITY, WHETHER IN AN ACTION OF CONTRACT, TORT OR OTHERWISE, ARISING FROM, OUT OF OR IN CONNECTION WITH THE SOFTWARE OR THE USE OR OTHER DEALINGS IN THE SOFTWARE.
messages.terms.measurements.title: About the measurements
messages.terms.measurements.p1: Results are measured from your computer. Wi-Fi signal, other devices on your network, a firewall, or the computer going to sleep can all affect them. Reports are a record of what your computer saw, not a certified measurement, and your provider may or may not accept them.
messages.terms.fair.title: Use it fairly
messages.terms.fair.p1: Only point checks and speed tests at servers you're allowed to use. Don't set very short intervals against servers you don't run. When you use Cloudflare, GitHub, Discord, Slack or Telegram through the app, their own terms apply.
messages.terms.changes.title: Changes
messages.terms.changes.p1: These terms may change in a new version. The date at the top shows the last update, and changes are listed in What's new.
messages.terms.contact.title: Questions
messages.terms.contact.p1: Reach us through any channel on the Contact page.
messages.about.story.1: Internet Monitor started with a familiar problem: the internet keeps dropping, and your provider says the line is fine. Without a record, it's your word against theirs.
messages.about.story.2: So the app watches your connection quietly in the background, records every outage with its exact time, length and cause, and turns that into a report you can send. It also tells you whether the problem is in your home network or at your provider, so you know who to call.
messages.about.principle.local.title: Your data stays with you
messages.about.principle.local.body: Everything is stored on your computer. No account, no cloud, no tracking.
messages.about.principle.open.title: Free and open source
messages.about.principle.open.body: MIT licensed, free for personal and commercial use. Anyone can read the code.
messages.about.principle.proof.title: Evidence, not guesses
messages.about.principle.proof.body: Exact times, durations and the layer that failed, ready for a PDF or CSV.
messages.about.principle.bilingual.title: Arabic and English
messages.about.principle.bilingual.body: Every screen, alert and report works in both languages, right to left included.
